item.title: LLM-Assisted Bi-Approximate CHC Solving
item.description: arXiv:2610.23771v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Constrained Horn clause (CHC) solvers often struggle to discover deep counterexamples whose derivations may require extensive rule unfolding. Although large language models (LLMs) can propose long-range symbolic relations, prior work on formally checked LLM-assisted verification has mainly focused on generating inductive invariants and concrete traces. We exploit this broader capability through Derivation Power Under-approximations (DPUs). Each DPU is a solver-certified under-approximation of the relation induced by a multi-step CHC derivation. An LLM proposes each DPU with symbolic intermediate-state witnesses that enable SMT validation without introducing additional quantifiers. Validated DPUs can be composed and reused soundly. Building on this mechanism, our LLM-assisted framework HornCraft combines invariant generation for over-approximation with DPU generation for under-approximation in CHC solving. On 260 linear and nonlinear integer-arithmetic CHC-COMP benchmarks left unresolved by a 30-minute Spacer run, HornCraft returns certified verdicts for 228 instances. It certifies 42 instances as unsafe, compared with 22 when DPU construction and reuse are disabled.
item.dc:creator: Baiting Jiang

item.title: A generalised and modular proof-theoretic semantics for sequent systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.23822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Base-extension semantics explains logical consequence via derivability in atomic systems. Extending this approach across logics requires careful control of structural principles and contexts. We present a modular sequent-based framework in which support is indexed by multisets of atomic resources and the semantic clauses for connectives are guided by their left introduction rules. The framework separates additive from multiplicative behaviour and makes explicit the contributions of structural rules and restrictions on sequents. We establish soundness and completeness for classical and intuitionistic propositional logic and for multiplicative-additive fragments of classical and intuitionistic linear logic. We then investigate axiomatic extensions of intuitionistic logic through Jankov logic. Two classes of atomic bases yield sound and complete semantics. Completeness is proven using two novel and modular methods using simulation bases, one of which is constructive. These results provide a common semantic treatment of several logical systems while identifying the additional conditions needed to extend the framework beyond structural variations.
item.dc:creator: Victor Barroso-Nascimento, Arghya Chakrabarty, Elaine Pimentel

item.title: Refusal Is Not Robustness: Measuring Harmful Reachability in Autoregressive Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.22754v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM safety evaluations via jailbreaking typically index on attack success rate (ASR): whether a generated response violates safeguards. However, ASR only evaluates sampled outputs and provides little information on the underlying generation process. Autoregressive language models define distributions over possible outputs, and a sampled refusal can coexist with substantial probability mass on harmful generation paths. We study this hidden structure through bounded continuation analysis (BCA), which models autoregressive generation as a stochastic process over token prefixes and computes the finite-horizon probability that generation reaches a harmful continuation. BCA constructs a bounded continuation tree, labels terminal continuations with a semantic harm evaluator, and estimates harmful reachability using exact probabilistic model checking. BCA complements ASR by measuring how much harmful behavior remains accessible beneath a sampled safe response. This makes it useful for distinguishing models that look identical under measured ASR values, and allocating red-team effort toward regions of the generation process with greater hidden risk. Across four instruction-tuned LLMs and 100 JailbreakBench behaviors, we show that BCA effectively quantifies hidden harmful behavior and provides a useful signal to guide red teaming.
item.dc:creator: Parv Kapoor, Teresa Fortes, Claudia Mamede, Rui Abreu, Jonathan Aldrich, Eunsuk Kang

item.title: Controlled PROP: Theory and Applications to Quantum Circuits
item.description: arXiv:2610.23192v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Control is a fundamental concept in quantum and reversible computational models. It enables the conditional application of a transformation to a system, depending on the state of another system. We introduce a general framework for diagrammatic reasoning featuring control as a constructor. To this end, we provide an elementary axiomatization of control functors, extending the standard formalism of PROPs to controlled PROPs. As an application, we show that controlled PROPs facilitate diagrammatic reasoning for quantum circuits. In particular, they admit a simple and complete axiomatization involving at most three qubits, whereas in the standard PROP setting, completeness necessarily requires axioms involving arbitrarily many qubits.
item.dc:creator: No\'e Delorme, Simon Perdrix

item.title: Model Checking for Noisy Toric Words
item.description: arXiv:2610.23463v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Toric words have recently gained attention as a means to model the behaviour of dynamical systems such as linear loops. This work is concerned with describing when the toric model is precise enough to decide whether the trace of a system is contained in an omega-regular language. Our contributions are threefold. (i) We use topological means to generalise a class of toric words by defining noise-robust dynamical systems and their sets of noisy traces. We prove that all noisy traces of a system are almost-periodic, and have the same set of recurrent factors. (ii) We apply the abstract techniques above to concrete sequences obtained as sign descriptions of real algebraic linear recurrence sequences (LRS), and show that the language-membership problem for sign descriptions of LRS with few dominant roots is decidable. (iii) We show that noisy traces of noise-robust dynamical systems are indistinguishable to a prefix-independent omega-regular language, and inclusion is decidable provided the common language of their recurrent factors is recursive. We incidentally obtain properties of prefix-independent omega-regular languages that may be of independent interest.
item.dc:creator: Mihir Vahanwala

item.title: SparseMax-dSTL: Sound Robustness with Horizon-Independent Gradient Allocation for Temporal Logic Trajectory Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.23837v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A gradient-based solver that enforces a Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specification uses a smooth approximation of its quantitative semantics, the robustness. In safety-critical trajectory optimization, this approximation must have two properties. First, it must be sound, that is, nonnegative only on trajectories that satisfy the specification. Second, at each temporal operator, the weight of its gradient on the violating samples must stay bounded away from zero, however long the horizon. The approximations in use, including the log-sum-exp, its sound variant, and the generalized-mean robustness, do not have both. We introduce lower approximations of the minimum and the maximum whose gradients are sparsemax projections, and we prove that the robustness built from them has both. It lies below the exact robustness and is therefore sound, and its error has a bound that is independent of the number of samples and known before optimization. The gradient of each approximation is exactly zero on every sample beyond a data-dependent threshold, so the weight on violating samples a gap beyond the others has a positive lower bound at every horizon. On a planar unicycle and on a seven-joint manipulator beside a person in simulation, the log-sum-exp approximation is positive on a violating trajectory. As the horizon of the manipulator's task grows from 10 to 80 s, the gradient weight of the sound variant on the violating samples falls from 0.22 to 0.04, while that of sparsemax stays at 1. In a constrained trajectory optimization of the unicycle, the constraint on the log-sum-exp robustness returns a violating trajectory, whereas the constraint on the sparsemax robustness returns a trajectory that satisfies the specification with the required margin.
item.dc:creator: Sai Sandeep Damera, Ryan Matheu, John S. Baras, Calin Belta

item.title: Decisiveness for countable MDPs and insights for NPLCSs and POMDPs
item.description: arXiv:2008.10426v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Markov chains and Markov decision processes (MDPs) are well-established probabilistic models. While finite Markov models are well-understood, analysing their infinite counterparts remains a significant challenge. Decisiveness has proved to be an elegant property for countable Markov chains: it is general enough to be satisfied by several natural classes of countable Markov chains, and it guarantees the termination of simple qualitative and approximate quantitative model-checking algorithms. In contrast, existing work on the formal analysis of countable MDPs usually relies on ad hoc techniques tailored to specific classes. In this paper, we provide a general framework to analyse countable MDPs (with finitely many enabled actions per state) by extending the notion of decisiveness. Compared to Markov chains, MDPs exhibit an additional nondeterministic choice that can be resolved in an adversarial or cooperative way, leading to multiple natural notions of decisiveness. We show that these notions enable the approximation of supremum reachability and infimum reachability (equivalently, supremum safety) probabilities in countable MDPs using generic approximation schemes. We then instantiate our generic approach to two concrete classes of models inducing countable MDPs: nondeterministic probabilistic lossy channel systems (NPLCSs) and partially observable MDPs (POMDPs). This leads to concrete algorithms to compute approximations to supremum safety probabilities in each of these classes.
item.dc:creator: Nathalie Bertrand, Patricia Bouyer, Thomas Brihaye, Paulin Fournier, Pierre Vandenhove

item.title: Complete Dynamic Logic of Communicating Hybrid Programs
item.description: arXiv:2408.05012v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This article presents a relatively complete proof calculus for the dynamic logic of communicating hybrid programs dLCHP. Beyond hybrid systems, communicating hybrid programs not only feature mixed discrete and continuous dynamics but also their parallel interactions in parallel hybrid systems. This not only combines the subtleties of hybrid and discrete parallel systems, but parallel hybrid dynamics necessitates that all parallel subsystems synchronize in time and evolve truly simultaneously. To enable compositional reasoning nevertheless, dLCHP combines differential dynamic logic dL with mutual abstraction of subsystems by assumption-commitment (ac) reasoning. The resulting proof calculus preserves the essence of dynamic logic axiomatizations, while revealing-and being driven by-a new modal logic view onto ac-reasoning. The dLCHP proof calculus is shown to be complete relative to $\Omega$-FOD, the first-order logic of differential equation properties FOD augmented with communication traces. This confirms that the calculus covers all aspects of parallel hybrid systems, because it lacks no axioms to reduce all their dynamical effects to the assertion logic. Additional axioms for encoding communication traces enable a provably correct equitranslation between $\Omega$-FOD and FOD, which reveals the possibility of representational succinctness in parallel hybrid systems proofs. Transitively, this establishes a full proof-theoretical alignment of dLCHP and dL, and shows that reasoning about parallel hybrid systems is exactly as hard as reasoning about hybrid systems, continuous systems, or discrete systems.
item.dc:creator: Marvin Brieger, Stefan Mitsch, Andr\'e Platzer

item.title: Synthesis of Infinite State Systems
item.description: arXiv:2501.08713v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The classical Church synthesis problem, solved by Buchi and Landweber, treats the synthesis of finite state systems. The synthesis of infinite state systems, on the other hand, has only been investigated few times since then, with no complete or systematic solution. We present a systematic study of the synthesis of infinite state systems. The main step involves the synthesis of MSO-definable parity games, which is, finding MSO-definable uniform memoryless winning strategies for these games.
item.dc:creator: Ohad Drucker, Alexander Rabinovich

item.title: Layered Monoidal Theories I: Diagrammatic Algebra and Applications
item.description: arXiv:2602.19776v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop layered monoidal theories -- a generalisation of monoidal theories combining formal descriptions of a system at different levels of abstraction. Via their representation as string diagrams, monoidal theories provide a graphical formalism to reason algebraically about information flow in models across different fields of science. Layered monoidal theories allow mixing several monoidal theories (together with translations between them) within the same string diagram, while retaining mathematical precision and semantic interpretability. We develop the mathematical foundations of layered monoidal theories, as well as providing several instances of our approach, including digital and electrical circuits, quantum processes, chemical reactions, concurrent processes, and probability theory.
item.dc:creator: Leo Lobski, Fabio Zanasi

item.title: A unification of graded and substructural logics
item.description: arXiv:2605.17112v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Type systems which account for resource sensitive computations can generally be split into two styles: First, substructural logics such as Linear Logic which seek to restrict weakening and contraction and reintroduce them in a controlled manner; And second, graded systems which allow weakening and contraction by default, but track the use of variables quantitatively in some algebraic structure -- usually a semiring. We present GRASS (Graded and substructural), a type system which incorporates mechanisms from both of these approaches, thus allowing maximally flexible control over variable usage. Furthermore, GRASS allows grades from an arbitrary collection of grade algebras to coexist in the same system, thus allowing different variables to be controlled with respect to different notions of resource within the same program. We develop the categorical semantics of GRASS, and find that, on the level of categorical semantics, it subsumes multiple established systems such as LNL, Adjoint Logic, and mGL.
item.dc:creator: Peter Hanukaev, Harley Eades III

item.title: A Gradient-Optimized TSK Fuzzy Framework for Explainable Phishing Detection
item.description: arXiv:2504.18636v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Phishing attacks represent an increasingly sophisticated and pervasive threat to individuals and organizations, causing significant financial losses, identity theft, and severe damage to institutional reputations. Existing phishing detection methods often struggle to simultaneously achieve high accuracy and explainability, either failing to detect novel attacks or operating as opaque black-box models. To address this critical gap, we propose a novel phishing URL detection system based on a first-order Takagi-Sugeno-Kang (TSK) fuzzy inference model optimized through gradient-based techniques. Our approach intelligently combines the interpretability and human-like reasoning capabilities of fuzzy logic with the precision and adaptability provided by gradient optimization methods, specifically leveraging the Adam optimizer for efficient parameter tuning. Experiments conducted using a comprehensive dataset of over 235,000 URLs demonstrate rapid convergence, exceptional predictive performance (accuracy averaging 99.95% across 5 cross-validation folds, with a perfect AUC i.e. 1.00). Furthermore, optimized fuzzy rules and membership functions improve interoperability, clearly indicating how the model makes decisions - an essential feature for cybersecurity applications. This high-performance, transparent, and interpretable phishing detection framework significantly advances current cybersecurity defenses, providing practitioners with accurate and explainable decision-making tools.
item.dc:creator: Lohith Srikanth Pentapalli, Jon Salisbury, Josette Riep, Kelly Cohen

item.title: Beyond Compilation: Evaluating Faithful Natural-Language-to-Lean Statement Formalization
item.description: arXiv:2606.31002v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Lean verifies that a generated declaration is well typed, but cannot check whether it states what the user intended. We measure how far compilation overstates faithfulness in statement autoformalization without canonical Lean targets. Our criterion requires Lean compilation and agreement of two LLM judges from different model families. On an independent random audit, it agrees with the human majority on 91.5% of cases; it rarely accepts an unfaithful output but rejects some faithful ones. Across eight systems on 227 university-level statements, the gap between compiling and accepted outputs ranges from 1.3 to 29.5 percentage points: our tool-augmented agent compiles 87.2% of the statements, but only 57.7% are accepted. Human review of all the agent's rejections confirms that 23.8 of its 29.5 points are real translation errors. For the gaps of the seven one-shot systems, a two-stage review by Claude Opus 5.5 with Lean and GPT-6.1 Sol, validated on these human labels, finds that 78-100% are real translation errors for six of them. When GPT-5.2, one of the two judges, grades the translations of two models released after it, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, it accepts 83% of the statements for each, against 21% for one-shot GPT-5.2. For these two models, the same review classifies only 4 of their 54 rejections (7%) as translation errors, so most of their measured gap is judge errors rather than translation errors. This is consistent with these systems erring less while the judge does not: the fewer errors a system makes, the smaller the share of its rejections that are translation errors. Finally, a 2^3 tool ablation of the agent shows that Lean feedback drives most of its compilation gain, and that nearly half of this gain fails the semantic criterion. Code and data are available at https://github.com/grenadeComing/beyond-compilation.
item.dc:creator: Ke Zhang, Patricio Gallardo Candela, Sudhir Murthy, Yi Xie, Zhi Wang, Maziar Raissi

item.title: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification
item.description: arXiv:2610.17697v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI systems now write long and difficult mathematical proofs, and checking their step-by-step validity is becoming a bottleneck. A learned verifier could check proofs cheaply, but training one requires a correctness label on every step, and such labels are hard to obtain for open-ended proofs. Existing methods take them from human annotators, which is costly, or derive them from final answers, which proofs do not have, and formalizing each proof in Lean requires expert effort. We introduce LeanPRM, a framework that uses the Lean proof assistant to create step-level labels for natural-language proofs. A model writes a natural-language proof together with a paired formal proof, without feedback from Lean. Lean then labels every step, and a second model discards failures caused only by the formal syntax, so that the negative labels mark errors in the mathematics. LeanPRM contains 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. A Qwen3-4B verifier trained on LeanPRM raises exact step-label accuracy on a held-out set of 200 proofs (LeanPRM-Bench) from 48.2 to 74.7, as opposed to 60.3 when the same base model is trained on PRM800K. It also selects better proofs in best-of-N selection on IMO-level problems, and outperforms the PRM800K-trained verifier on three of four external verification benchmarks. Training on LeanPRM improves verifiers at every size from 0.6B to 8B parameters on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench. Given the labels need no human annotation, LeanPRM can grow with the supply of formal statements, offering a path to step-level feedback on AI-generated proofs that are hard for humans to check.
item.dc:creator: Rodney Lafuente-Mercado, Salman Rahman, Jingyan Shen, James Shiffer, Saadia Gabriel, Pavel Izmailov
